title_en: The Standing-Places of the Resurrection and the Signs of the Hour
body_ar:
اليوم الآخر هو اليوم الذي يجتمع فيه جميع الخلق، وتنكشف فيه الحقائق، ويجازى كل مخلوق بما يستحق، وقد جعل الله له علامات يعرف قرب وقوعه بها، فما على المسلم إلا الإيمان به والعمل له.
معنى اليوم الآخر:
بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم الحمد لله رب العالمين، وأصلي وأسلم على من بعث رحمة للعالمين، وعلى آله وأصحابه ومن اهتدى بهديه واستن بسنته إلى يوم الدين. أما بعد: فيقول الشيخ حفظه الله تعالى: [واليوم الاخر وما قد اشتمل عليه من حشر وعرض لعمل حق كذا الوزن وما به التحق والنار حق وكذا الجنة حق] من أركان الإيمان الإيمان باليوم الآخر، واليوم في الدنيا هو الوحدة الزمنية المعروفة، وأطلق على الآخرة باعتبار اتصاله وعدم انقطاعه، فكأنه يوم واحد وإن كان قدره آلاف السنين: وَإِنَّ يَوْمًا عِنْدَ رَبِّكَ كَأَلْفِ سَنَةٍ مِمَّا تَعُدُّونَ [الحج:47]...
body_en:
*[Site synopsis]* The Last Day is the day on which all creation is gathered together, on which the realities are laid bare, and on which every created being is recompensed with what it deserves. God has appointed signs for it by which the nearness of its coming may be known; and nothing is required of the Muslim but to believe in it and to work for it.

## The meaning of the Last Day

In the name of God, the All-Merciful, the Mercy-Giving. Praise belongs to God, Lord of the worlds. I ask God's blessing and peace upon the one sent as a mercy to the worlds, and upon his family and his Companions, and upon all who have taken guidance from his guidance and followed his practice until the Day of Judgement. To proceed: the Sheikh, may God preserve him, says: *[And the Last Day, and what it has comprised of the gathering and of the presentation of deeds, is true; so too the weighing and what is attached to it; and the Fire is true, and likewise the Garden is true.]*

Among the pillars of faith is faith in the Last Day. "Day" in this world is the familiar unit of time, and it was applied to the hereafter in view of its being continuous and unbroken, so that it is as though it were a single day, even if its measure is thousands of years: {And indeed a day with your Lord is as a thousand years of what you count} (Sūrat al-Ḥajj 22:47) …

flags.context: the record breaks off and the full text sits behind a download
options: render with an excerpt banner and link the .doc
flags.note: Excerpt only, style guide section 9. It breaks off on an ellipsis while still glossing the word 'day', so that neither the standing-places of the Resurrection nor the signs of the Hour — the two subjects of the title — is reached at all. The complete text sits behind /medias/doc/L-39.doc. The English ends exactly where the Arabic ends and completes nothing. Must not be rendered as a whole lesson.

flags.arabic: الفقرة الافتتاحية مقابل ما بعد العنوان الفرعي
flags.context: the synopsis paragraph against the transcribed opening of the lesson
options: mark the synopsis as the site's own and the remainder as the Sheikh's words
present the whole record as the Sheikh's words
flags.note: The record has two authors. The first paragraph is a synopsis written by the site — it speaks about the lesson and its subject in the third person and does not begin with the opening formula. Everything from the section heading onward is transcribed speech in the Sheikh's own voice. The site must not present the synopsis as his words.

flags.context: the formula introducing each quoted line of the versified creed being commented on
options: read it as the author of the versified base text, distinct from the lecturer
read it as Sheikh al-Dedew quoting his own verse
flags.note: Getting this referent wrong would misattribute a creedal formulation, so it is flagged on every record in which the formula appears. These lessons are a commentary on a versified creed (nazm): the transcriber introduces each base-text line with 'the Sheikh, may God preserve him, said', and the commentary follows. 'حفظه الله' is used of the living, which at first sight fits Sheikh al-Dedew himself. Three passages inside the run settle it otherwise. Record 719 has the speaker giving thanks for 'completing the commentary on the Sheikh's versification' and describing what 'the Sheikh' chose to leave undetailed — a commentator does not ordinarily speak of his own base text that way while expounding it. Record 716 describes the base text as a versification of the Mukhtaṣar of Khalil ibn Ishaq by 'one of the scholars'. Record 718 introduces the same quoted lines with 'the versifier said'. The reading adopted throughout this slice is therefore that 'the Sheikh' is the living author of the versified base text and the lecturer is his commentator. The author is nowhere named, and the identification should be confirmed by the Sheikh's office before publication, because the bracketed verse and the prose around it carry different attributions.

flags.arabic: فما على المسلم إلا الإيمان به والعمل له
flags.context: the closing clause of the site's synopsis
options: nothing is required of the Muslim but to believe in it and to work for it
the Muslim has only to believe in it and act for it
it is incumbent on the Muslim to believe in it and to work for it
flags.note: 'ما على المسلم إلا' is a restrictive construction — what is upon him is this and nothing further — and the English keeps the restriction. The third option states an obligation without the restriction and would be a different sentence. Note that the construction does state a duty, but by exclusion, and no ruling word from the fixed table appears.

flags.context: in the quoted line of verse
options: preserve the source's spelling without the hamzah and translate the evident word
flags.note: SOURCE DEFECT, style guide section 11. The verse is served with 'الاخر' lacking its madda, while the prose two clauses later has 'الآخر' correctly. A transcription artefact of the same class as those in records 707 and 708 of this run. Preserved in body_ar and not repaired.

flags.arabic: وعرض لعمل حق كذا الوزن وما به التحق
flags.context: the quoted line of the versified base text
options: and of the presentation of deeds, is true; so too the weighing and what is attached to it
and the presentation of deeds is true, as is the weighing and whatever joins it
and the display of works, is true; likewise the scales and what belongs with them
flags.note: The line lists the events of the Last Day and affirms each as true: the gathering (ḥashr), the presentation of deeds (ʿarḍ), the weighing (wazn) and 'what is attached to it'. The scope of 'حق' across the list, and the referent of 'ما به التحق', are both elliptical in the verse, and the English is provisional. 'الوزن' is the weighing of deeds; rendering it 'the scales' would name the instrument where the Arabic names the act.

flags.context: the second half of the title
flags.note: 'أشراط' is the established term for the signs preceding the Hour, Qur'anic at Sūrat Muhammad 47:18. 'Conditions' would be a false friend from the other sense of the root. The synopsis uses the plainer 'علامات' for the same thing, and both are rendered 'signs'.

translator_notes: One of a run of fifteen records, IDs 707-721, in the written-creed section, all uploaded on 9 and 10 May 2011 within a few hours of one another, all built to the same template and all excerpts. Each carries a site-written synopsis, then a section heading, then the opening formula and the first lines of a lesson, and then breaks off on an ellipsis; the full text sits behind a .doc download in the /medias/doc/L-* series, numbered L-26 to L-39 in the same order as the IDs. The uniform timestamps are a bulk upload and say nothing about when the lesson was delivered.

The record contains two distinct voices and the English keeps them apart. The opening paragraph is a synopsis written by the site, about the lesson and in the third person; everything from the section heading onward is the Sheikh's own words as transcribed. Nothing in the synopsis may be quoted as his.

The source's final line, 'تحميل المادة' ('download the material'), is the label of a download link in the page furniture, not part of the text. It is recorded as source_download_link and omitted from body_ar and body_en.

The base text being commented on is identified inside this run. Record 719 has the Sheikh speaking of 'completing the commentary on the Sheikh's versification', and of that versifier's rendering of Khalil's Jāmiʿ in some five hundred lines; record 716 describes the base text as a versification of the Mukhtaṣar of Khalil ibn Ishaq whose opening section is on creed; and record 718 introduces the same quoted lines with 'the versifier said'. Taken together these settle that 'the Sheikh, may God preserve him' in this run is the living author of the versified base text and not the lecturer. The author is never named.
The last record of the creed run. Like most of the run it delivers the opening formula, one quoted line of the base text and the first sentences of commentary, and then stops.
The English breaks the transcribed portion into two paragraphs where the source runs on, separating the quoted verse from the commentary. No word has been added or removed.
No ruling term from the five-rulings table appears anywhere in the record.
